references.text: The Jews persecuted Jesus not only because he healed on the Sabbath, but also because he called God his own Father and thereby made himself equal to God ([ref:Joh 5:18|John 5:18]).
The Jewish persecution of Jesus continued, and he avoided traveling in Judea because they wanted to kill him ([ref:Joh 7:1|John 7:1]).

Jesus defends his Sabbath healing by pointing out that the Jews themselves perform circumcision on the Sabbath, so why are they then angry with him because he healed a whole person on the Sabbath? ([ref:Joh 7:23|John 7:23])
Also in the healing of the man born blind, the Pharisees accused Jesus of breaking the Sabbath ([ref:Joh 9:16|John 9:16]).
The Pharisees accused Jesus' disciples of doing what is not allowed on the Sabbath, which shows the recurring conflict theme surrounding the Sabbath ([ref:Matt 12:2|Matthew 12:2]).
After Jesus healed the man with the withered hand on the Sabbath, the Pharisees made plans to take his life ([ref:Mark 3:6|Mark 3:6]).
The scribes and Pharisees watched Jesus closely to see if he would heal on the Sabbath, so that they could find something to accuse him of ([ref:Luk 6:7|Luke 6:7]).
The synagogue ruler became angry because Jesus healed on the Sabbath, and said that people should come to be healed on the six working days ([ref:Luk 13:14|Luke 13:14]).
The Sabbath commandment in the Ten Commandments forbids work on the seventh day, and it was this commandment the Jews believed Jesus broke ([ref:2 Mos 20:10|Exodus 20:10]).
The penalty for breaking the Sabbath under the old covenant was death, as illustrated by the man who gathered wood on the Sabbath ([ref:4 Mos 15:32-36|Numbers 15:32-36]).
The conflict began when the Jews told the healed man that it was not allowed to carry his bed on the Sabbath ([ref:Joh 5:10|John 5:10]).
The prophet Jeremiah conveys the Lord's command not to carry any burden on the Sabbath day, which the Jews accused the healed man of breaking ([ref:Jer 17:21-22|Jeremiah 17:21-22]).
